Summary and sentiment (incorporating SLOOS):
- The May 4, 2022 FOMC statement is hawkish: inflation is elevated, Ukraine and China-related supply disruptions add upside inflation risk and downside growth risk; the Committee raised the funds rate to 0.75–1.00% and set QT to begin June 1.
- The May 2022 FSR corroborates these headwinds, flagging geopolitical risks, higher energy prices, funding and cyber risks, and the drag from tighter policy, but notes resilient household credit metrics and strong bank capital/liquidity with limited Russia exposure.
- The April 2022 SLOOS points to more supportive domestic credit conditions than the FSR alone implies: banks on net eased standards for C&I loans and multifamily properties, left construction/land/nonfarm nonresidential standards mostly unchanged, and reported stronger demand for C&I credit (inventory, A/R, plant and equipment) while reducing the cost of credit lines. For households, banks reported weaker demand for RRE mortgages but stronger demand for HELOCs and auto loans; foreign banks tightened C&I standards.
- Net effect: Macro and geopolitical risks plus policy tightening keep the tone negative, but SLOOS evidence of easing domestic bank standards and stronger credit demand tempers the downside. Adjusting for SLOOS, the overall tone is slightly negative but less so than FSR alone.
